description: A two-panel schematic (no axes, no scale bars, no printed numbers) illustrating crack propagation in Fe–20Mn–9Al–1.5C–2Ni–3Cr low-density steel. (a) A 3D cut-away block of pale-blue polygonal grains labelled S1000; a red dashed ellipse on the front face is magnified into a circular inset via yellow dashed arrows. A thick white jagged line, annotated in red text "Crack propagation path" with a red arrow, traverses both block and inset. The (a) inset labels austenite grains "γ" in yellow, a particle phase "θ" in yellow, and short red boundary segments annotated "RB" and a further red label that is only partially legible. (b) The equivalent block and inset for MHT: the white crack path is visibly more tortuous, deflecting repeatedly from boundary to boundary, and the grains appear coarser/fewer. The (b) inset again labels "γ" in yellow and shows red boundary segments, one carrying a short label that appears to read "Σ9". Both panels share the same colour code (blue grains, black dashed internal lines, red dashed zoom circles, yellow zoom arrows), making the argument visual: the random high-angle boundaries of S1000 give a shorter, straighter crack, whereas the special boundaries of MHT force a longer, deflected path.

subfigures.description: 3D block schematic of a polygonal grain structure (S1000) with a red dashed ellipse on the front face magnified into a circular inset; a thick white jagged line labelled in red 'Crack propagation path' runs through block and inset. Inset labels: yellow 'γ' (austenite grains), yellow 'θ' (particles), red boundary segments labelled 'RB' and a second red label that is only partially legible; short dashed lines mark boundary types.

Equivalent 3D block schematic for MHT with a larger red dashed ellipse and a coarser grain structure; the white 'Crack propagation path' line is markedly more tortuous, changing direction many times. The circular inset labels 'γ' in yellow and shows red boundary segments, one with a short label that appears to read 'Σ9'.

observations.observation: The figure consists of two side-by-side 3D block schematics of polygonal grain structures, each with a red dashed circle/ellipse marking a region that is enlarged into a circular inset (linked by yellow dashed arrows).
In each panel a thick white jagged line is annotated with red text 'Crack propagation path' and a red arrow, identifying it as the crack trajectory.

The (a) inset labels austenite grains 'γ' in yellow and a particle phase 'θ' in yellow, and marks red boundary segments with the annotation 'RB' (a further red label in the same inset is only partially legible).
The (b) inset labels 'γ' in yellow and contains a red-marked boundary whose short label appears to read 'Σ9'; this label is small and only tentatively readable.
The white crack path in (b) makes more direction changes and follows more boundary segments than the path in (a), which is comparatively straight.
The grain polygons drawn in the (b) block are fewer and larger than those in the (a) block, and the red dashed zoom ellipse in (b) is larger.
No axes, scale bars or printed numerical values appear anywhere in the figure.
The caption states the schematic shows crack propagation with differences in the grain boundaries in (a) S1000 and (b) MHT.

The citing text states that for S1000 cracks propagate rapidly along the random high-angle boundaries despite a high percentage of special boundaries, and that cracks tend to nucleate at grain boundaries because of precipitates at the boundaries.

The citing text states that in MHT the precipitates at the grain boundary disappear and that increasing grain size and frequency of special boundaries cause crack propagation to be hindered by low-energy special boundaries within the austenite grains.

The citing text states that crack paths in MHT are deflected along special boundaries, that the number of propagation paths increases, and that this increases energy consumption and improves impact toughness.

The citing text defines the impact process as crack initiation (start point to maximum load F_m) and crack propagation (F_m to fracture), with the corresponding areas being the crack initiation and propagation energies.
